content: Pseudoephedrine, commonly abbreviated as PSE, is a sympathomimetic amine widely used as a decongestant. It is available in the form of pseudoephedrine hydrochloride and pseudoephedrine sulfate salts, which are found in many over-the-counter medications. These formulations may be single-ingredient products or, more commonly, combined with antihistamines, paracetamol, and/or ibuprofen. In North America, the United Kingdom, and Australia, pseudoephedrine is often referred to by the brand name Sudafed, although Pfizer now markets Sudafed PE, which does not contain pseudoephedrine. Unlike antihistamines, which target systemic histamine-mediated allergic responses, pseudoephedrine primarily alleviates nasal congestion associated with colds or allergies. Some users report additional relief from symptoms such as itchy or watery eyes, which may not respond effectively to antihistamines. Oral pseudoephedrine has an advantage over topical nasal decongestants like oxymetazoline, as it does not cause rebound congestion (rhinitis medicamentosa). However, it is more likely to cause systemic side effects, including hypertension. Chemistry Pseudoephedrine is a phenethylamine and a diastereomer of ephedrine. It is a chiral molecule, existing in both left-handed and right-handed configurations that are not superimposable. The International Nonproprietary Name (INN) for pseudoephedrine refers to the (1S, 2S)-diastereomer of ephedrine. Other names include (+)-pseudoephedrine and D-pseudoephedrine. The optical isomer, L-pseudoephedrine (or (-)-(1R, 2R)-pseudoephedrine), has fewer side effects, reduced central nervous system (CNS) stimulatory effects, and does not convert to D-methamphetamine, yet retains its efficacy as a decongestant. However, L-pseudoephedrine has not been approved for public sale by its patent holder (Pfizer/Warner-Lambert). Mode of Action Pseudoephedrine acts as a sympathomimetic amine, primarily exerting its effects through indirect action on the adrenergic receptor system. While it may have weak agonist activity at αand β-adrenergic receptors, its main mechanism involves displacing noradrenaline from storage vesicles in presynaptic neurons. The released noradrenaline activates postsynaptic adrenergic receptors, which are located on the smooth muscles lining blood vessel walls. This activation causes vasoconstriction, reducing the amount of fluid leaving the blood vessels and entering the nasal, throat, and sinus linings. Consequently, inflammation of nasal membranes and mucus production are decreased. The vasoconstriction primarily involves α-adrenergic receptor responses and leads to reduced nasal congestion. Pseudoephedrine demonstrates greater selectivity for nasal mucosa and lower affinity for CNS adrenergic receptors compared to other sympathomimetic amines. Additional benefits include improved sinus drainage and opening of obstructed Eustachian tubes. However, the vasoconstriction can also result in hypertension, a noted side effect. Clinical Use Indications Pseudoephedrine is indicated for the treatment of: Nasal congestion Sinus congestion Eustachian tube congestion It is also used for vasomotor rhinitis and as an adjunct in the treatment of allergic rhinitis, croup, sinusitis, otitis media, and tracheobronchitis. Additionally, pseudoephedrine is employed as a first-line therapy for priapism, leveraging its sympathetic action to counteract the parasympathetic response responsible for the condition. An off-label use includes treatment for urinary incontinence, where it increases the tension of the bladder neck and urethral muscles, aiding in urine retention. Adverse Effects Common adverse drug reactions (ADRs) include CNS stimulation, sleeplessness, nervousness, excitability, dizziness, and anxiety. Less frequently, tachycardia and/or palpitations may occur. Rarely, pseudoephedrine therapy has been associated with hallucinations, arrhythmias, hypertension, seizures, and ischemic colitis. Severe skin reactions, such as recurrent pseudo-scarletina, systemic contact dermatitis, and non-pigmenting fixed drug eruptions, have also been reported. Precautions and Contraindications Pseudoephedrine should be used cautiously in patients with diabetes mellitus, cardiovascular disease, hypertension, prostatic hypertrophy, hyperthyroidism, closed-angle glaucoma, and/or pregnancy. Given that nasal congestion is a relatively minor ailment, alternative treatments such as topical decongestants or saline sprays are preferred for patients with these conditions. Contraindications include concurrent or recent (within 14 days) monoamine oxidase inhibitor (MAOI) therapy, severe or uncontrolled hypertension, and severe coronary artery disease. Individuals with bipolar disorder should exercise caution, as pseudoephedrine can cause insomnia and potentially trigger manic episodes. Chiral Auxiliary Both (R,R)and (S,S)-pseudoephedrine are used as chiral auxiliaries in chemical synthesis. Pseudoephedrine reacts with carboxylic acids, acid anhydrides, or acyl chlorides to form pseudoephedrine amides. The α-proton of the carbonyl compound is easily deprotonated by a non-nucleophilic base, forming an enolate that can undergo further reactions. The configuration of the addition product is directed by the methyl group, resulting in anti-addition to the methyl group and syn-addition to the hydroxyl group. The pseudoephedrine chiral auxiliary is subsequently removed by cleaving the amide bond with an appropriate nucleophile. Manufacture Pseudoephedrine occurs naturally as an alkaloid in certain plant species, such as Ephedra (Ma Huang), where it coexists with other ephedrine isomers. However, most commercially produced pseudoephedrine is derived from yeast fermentation of dextrose in the presence of benzaldehyde. Specialized yeast strains, such as Candida utilis or Saccharomyces cerevisiae, are used in large vats containing water, dextrose, and the enzyme pyruvate decarboxylase. Benzaldehyde is added during fermentation, and the yeast converts the precursors into L-phenylacetylcarbinol (L-PAC), which is then chemically converted to pseudoephedrine via reductive amination. The majority of pseudoephedrine is manufactured in India and China, where economic and industrial conditions favor mass production for export. Misuse and Illicit Use Pseudoephedrine has been misused for its stimulant properties. Some individuals, such as long-distance truck drivers and athletes, have reportedly used it to enhance alertness and wakefulness. However, its minimal CNS effects make it unlikely to provide significant benefit except in sensitive individuals. Misuse has been associated with stimulant dependence. Due to its structural similarity to amphetamines, pseudoephedrine is a sought-after precursor in the illicit production of methamphetamine and methcathinone. Consequently, regulatory restrictions on its sale and distribution have increased, prompting pharmaceutical companies to reformulate medications with alternative decongestants like phenylephrine. Retailers have implemented policies limiting purchase quantities and requiring proper identification, often exceeding legal requirements. International and Federal Regulations Internationally, pseudoephedrine is classified as a Schedule I precursor under the United Nations Convention Against Illicit Traffic in Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances. In the United States, the Combat Methamphetamine Epidemic Act of 2005 (CMEA) imposed strict regulations on the sale of pseudoephedrine-containing products, including record-keeping, purchase limits, and behind-the-counter storage. In Oregon, pseudoephedrine is classified as a Schedule III controlled substance, requiring a prescription for purchase. In Australia, pseudoephedrine products have been rescheduled as Pharmacist Only Medicines (Schedule 3), requiring direct pharmacist involvement in sales and online tracking of purchases through the PROJECT STOP database. Certain high-strength preparations are further restricted as Prescription Only Medicines (Schedule 4). The Australian government has considered banning all pseudoephedrine-containing medications. In New Zealand, pseudoephedrine-containing cold and flu medications are classified as Class C controlled drugs under the Misuse of Drugs Act 1975. Customs and police continue to intercept large quantities of precursor substances intended for methamphetamine production.
